outputs.L2: Through the creaky pantry door, we sneak boxes of Beaujolais. Cases of cigarettes vanish into our hands, and we commandeer the armored Mercedes to tear across the deserted streets of the capital. How lovely this quiet is. Not a single citizen here can afford a vehicle—only the police can. They stand around their cars, waving as we pass. Their vehicles sit useless, drained of fuel. Across the country, beer bottles have run out. There isn't a single bar anywhere. Getting drunk behind the wheel is our pastime; steering while stoned, our craft. Every last one of us in the bad girls' crew crowds into that Mercedes, with Vijay pounding the Ashanti drum the entire way to the shore. Cash means nothing here—cigarettes are the real currency. Stretched out across the sand, clutching our French wine and our Hong Kong blondes, we gaze up into the midnight heavens over the Atlantic Slave Coast: let all my diamonds glitter, because they really are diamonds.
outputs.L3:
# A Childhood on the Edge

We lived by our own rules, my companions and I, chasing danger as though it were a game with no consequences. We smuggled wine across borders, slipped cartons of stolen cigarettes into our pockets, and tore through the streets of the capital in a bulletproof Mercedes that gleamed obscenely against the crumbling backdrop of the city. The recklessness of it all felt like freedom, though it was really something closer to abandonment.

The country around us was a portrait of collapse. People here could not dream of owning cars; the very machine we drove would have represented several lifetimes of wages to the average citizen. Even the police were rendered helpless, their vehicles sitting idle for want of petrol, their authority hollowed out by the same scarcity that gripped everyone else. Shortages defined daily life, extending to the most ordinary of things—there were times when even empty beer bottles were treasured, impossible to come by.

The old economy had ceased to function in any meaningful way. Money had become little more than paper, its value evaporated, its promises broken. In its place, we traded in cigarettes. They were the true currency now, passed from hand to hand to purchase favors, goods, and silence. A single carton could accomplish what a wallet full of banknotes never could.

And I was thirteen years old.

It is a difficult thing to admit, even now—that a child of thirteen moved through this world of smuggling and stolen luxury, of bulletproof glass and blackmarket exchange. But that was the truth of it. We were children playing at the lives of criminals, too young to grasp how easily any of it could have ended us.

When the pressure of the city grew too heavy, we would escape to a rented hut along the coast. There we would open bottles of French wine and lie back, gazing up at the enormous sky. Below us stretched the Atlantic—the same waters that had, for centuries, borne the weight of unspeakable history along that stretch of shore once known as the Slave Coast. We drank and stared upward, small and oblivious, beneath a sky that had witnessed so much more than we could ever understand.
outputs.L4:
**The Girls of the Slave Coast**

They are thirteen, all of them, though they carry themselves like something older and harder—girls with sun-bleached hair and passports thick as prayer books, daughters of oilmen and ambassadors and men who deal in things that never appear on paper. The capital sprawls around them like a wound that will not close: red dust, corrugated tin, the ceaseless traffic of bodies moving toward some hope that keeps receding. Generators cough. The power comes and goes. On the horizon, the sea that once carried ships full of the chained now carries container vessels and the girls' fathers' business.

They do not think about this. Why would they.

Morning: a bulletproof Mercedes idling in a compound behind razor wire, the driver waiting, the air conditioning a small arctic miracle. They pile in with their bare brown legs and their laughter, and the tinted windows slide up, and the city becomes a silent film through the glass—a woman balancing a basin of water on her head, a boy with no shoe, a market blooming with color and flies. The car glides through it all untouched, a cold bubble of privilege on wheels.

Afternoon: they drive too fast on the coast road, someone's older brother's Land Cruiser, the speedometer trembling, the radio screaming French pop from Abidjan. They pass bottles of wine between them—real French wine, Bordeaux lifted from a father's cellar, drunk warm from the neck because none of them can be bothered with glasses. One of them wears diamonds. Actual diamonds, in her ears, at thirteen, winking in the equatorial light. She got them, she says, from a man who owed her father a favor, and she does not explain what the favor was and no one asks.

The smuggling is a game to them. Cartons of cigarettes, sometimes small packages wrapped in brown paper that they never look inside, tucked into their beach bags because who searches the beach bags of white girls in a country like this. They run these things across checkpoints with practiced innocence, batting their eyes at soldiers barely older than themselves, and they feel invincible, and they laugh about it after in that high hysterical register that is almost fear.

Evening belongs to the beach. Bonfires and imported vodka and boys who arrive from nowhere. They swim in the dark warm water, the same water, and they lie in the sand and watch the stars that are so much brighter here than in Europe, and they talk about nothing—about which of them is bored, which of them wants to go home, home being a place none of them can quite define. Behind the dunes, past the fringe of palms, the fishing villages sit in near-darkness, their children asleep on mats, their nets drying, their bellies empty.

The girls do not see the villages. Or they see them and see through them, the way you see furniture. This is the thing about them, the disturbing thing: not cruelty, exactly. Cruelty would require attention. It is the detachment, the flawless self-absorption of the very young and the very insulated, floating like an oil slick across the surface of a nation's deprivation—bright, iridescent, poisonous, and utterly unaware of the depth of the water beneath.

At thirteen. On a coast that remembers everything, and forgets nothing, except perhaps them.
outputs.L5:
# An Evening to Remember

There was something almost cinematic about the way the sunset draped itself over the vineyards that afternoon. **The** rolling hills of the Beaujolais region glowed a deep amber, the rows of Gamay grapes stretching toward the horizon like brushstrokes on a painter's canvas.

Henri had waited all year for this moment. Every autumn, he made the same pilgrimage from the city to the countryside, trading the noise of urban life for the quiet rhythm of harvest season. This year, however, felt different. This year, he arrived in style.

The gleaming silver **Mercedes** rolled to a gentle stop at the edge of the estate, its polished surface catching the last golden rays of the day. It was not just a car—it was a symbol of everything he had worked toward, a reward for years of patience and persistence. He stepped out, breathing in the earthy scent of the soil and the faint sweetness of ripening fruit.

Inside the old stone cellar, the winemaker was already uncorking a bottle of freshly pressed **Beaujolais**. The wine, young and vibrant, carried notes of cherry, raspberry, and a whisper of spring flowers. It was the kind of drink meant to be shared among friends, poured generously and enjoyed without pretense.

"To another good year," the winemaker said, raising his glass.

Henri smiled, thinking of the journey that had brought him here—the long roads, the quiet ambitions, and the simple pleasures that made it all worthwhile. Some evenings, he realized, were meant to be savored slowly, like the finest of wines.

And **the** memory of that day would linger with him long after the last drop was gone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short, impressionistic prose piece from the perspective of a rebellious 13-year-old expat girl living in a West African capital, capturing the surreal decadence and lawlessness of her world in vivid present-tense fragments.
counterfactuals.output:
The Dry Season

Morning comes yellow with dust. The Harmattan again, sifting the Sahara through our window screens, powdering the piano nobody plays.

I am thirteen and nobody watches me.

The guard sleeps in his plastic chair by the gate, mouth open, machete across his knees like a sleeping baby. Amadou. He calls me *petite* and lets me pass because I bring him cigarettes from Papa's carton, the good American ones, and what does Papa need with counting.

Outside the wall the road is red. Everything here is red or gold or rotting green. A woman balances a tower of oranges on her head and does not look at me, the white ghost girl in her brother's shorts, and I love her for not looking.

*

At the Club the wives drink gin before noon. Their sunglasses are enormous. They talk about the coup that might come, the way you'd talk about rain—will it, won't it, should we close the shutters. Mrs. Delacroix lost three fingers to something, nobody says what, and she stirs her drink with the stumps and laughs too loud and everyone pretends.

The pool is turquoise poison. I float on my back and watch the vultures ride the heat above the embassy, patient, patient.

*

Sixteen francs buys a warm Coke and a boy named Ousmane will drive you anywhere on his brother's moped. Anywhere. Down to the port where the tankers rust, past the presidential palace with its peacocks and its soldiers who are fourteen, younger than me, cradling guns bigger than their bodies. Their eyes slide over us. We are nothing to shoot today.

Ousmane says one day he'll go to Paris. Everyone here is going to Paris the way people are going to heaven—later, when the money comes, when God decides.

*

Night falls like a curtain dropped. No dusk. The generators cough on all along the boulevard and the diplomats' houses light up one by one, little kingdoms behind their glass and razor wire, while beyond them the whole dark city breathes and cooks and sings.

I climb out my window onto the flat roof. Below, my parents are having people—ice clinking, someone's laugh, the ambassador's wife saying *of course it's tragic but*—

Up here the stars are ridiculous. Obscene. So many.

Something is burning somewhere in the low quarter. There is always something burning. The sky over there glows soft orange like a second, dirtier dawn, and I watch it and feel it, that terrible sweet feeling, that this place is teaching me something my mother will never know.

That anything can happen here.

That I am the only one awake.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of experimental flash fiction about privileged teenagers in a collapsing African economy where cigarettes are currency and money is worthless. Use a breathless, run-on style.
counterfactuals.output:
# Marlboro Gold

We are rich, so rich, richer than God's own accountant, because Baba stockpiled before the collapse, three freezers full, and now when the maid quits crying and the pool goes green with algae we still have cartons, cartons stacked like gold bricks in the panic room, and Tumi says we should throw a party, so we throw a party, because what else is there when the numbers on the money went so big they stopped meaning anything, a billion for bread, a trillion for nothing, and the paper is better for lighting the barbecue than for buying it—

and everyone comes, everyone who's anyone still left, the Nkosi twins in their imported everything, and Lesedi who kissed me by the generator last December when there was still diesel to run it, and we are smoking not because we like it, God no, it's disgusting, it tastes like the future feels, but because you smoke your own wealth now, you inhale it, you flick the ash of your inheritance onto the imported Italian tile while outside the gate the man who used to wash Baba's cars stands very still, watching, one cigarette would feed his family for a week and we are burning them for fun, we are burning them because we can, because the burning is the point, the burning is the flex—

and Tumi lights one off another off another, chain-chain-chaining, laughing, and I want to tell him stop, stop, that's a month of somebody's life turning to smoke, but I don't, I don't say anything, because I have three in my mouth right now too, I am a chimney of privilege, I am exhaling somebody's medicine, somebody's schoolbook, somebody's next meal into the humid dark—

and then the lights go out, the last generator coughs and dies, and in the sudden blackness there are only the orange dots, dozens of them, floating like fireflies, like the eyes of small animals, like the last lit ends of everything we were given and never earned, and someone screams and someone laughs and I can't tell which of us it is anymore, in the dark we are all just glowing—

and beyond the wall I hear the gate, I hear the gate, I hear the gate.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness paragraph about smuggling, teenage recklessness, and colonial excess set on the Atlantic Slave Coast, ending with a defiant line about diamonds.
counterfactuals.output: The heat coming off the water was a living thing, thick as the molasses they'd bled from the factor's stores, and I was sixteen and stupid and certain I would live forever the way you only can when you've never watched anyone die slow, and the ships sat fat in the roadstead—Dutch, Portuguese, our own with their names like prayers nobody meant—and we ran the lagoons at night in a canoe that smelled of fish and gunpowder, ferrying rum past the excise men who took their cut in coin and looked the other way while the governor's house glittered up on the bluff with its chandeliers hauled across an ocean just to burn candles in a country that had more sun than God knew what to do with, and I remember the excess of it, the waste, the crystal and the mahogany and the wine poured out on the veranda while below the shoreline the whole coast was a wound that never closed, and we teenagers thought we were pirates, thought we were clever, thought the danger was a game because we hadn't yet understood whose blood paid for our little thrills, the ledgers thick with human names reduced to numbers, and my hands shaking not from fear but from the pure electric arrogance of being young and outrunning a musket ball, laughing, always laughing, until the laughter curdled into something I'd carry the rest of my days—and still, God help me, when the factor's daughter asked what I'd risk it all for, I looked her dead in her powdered face and said: diamonds, and let them hang every last one of us if they can catch us first.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a gritty, poetic vignette narrated by a member of a "bad girls' group" of diplomats' kids in an African city with no petrol, no bars, and a bulletproof Mercedes. Make it feel dreamlike and morally ambiguous.
counterfactuals.output:
The Petrol Girls

We were the daughters of men who signed things.

Treaties, mostly. Loan agreements written in a language none of the locals had voted for. Our fathers pressed pens to paper in cool rooms while we pressed our foreheads to the tinted glass of the Mercedes, watching the city bleed past in the heat.

There were four of us that season. Ines, whose mother had drunk herself back to Lisbon. Adaeze, who was technically home but treated her own country like a hotel with poor service. Mische, the Swede, so pale she seemed to be made of the light itself. And me. I don't give my name to stories. Names are how they find you.

There was no petrol that year. The pumps stood like dry cathedrals, and men slept beside them holding their place in lines that never moved. But our car ran. Somebody's father made sure of it. The Mercedes drank while the country thirsted, and we sat inside its cool leather belly, bulletproof, breathing filtered air, laughing at nothing.

That was the thing about us. We laughed at nothing because everything was too large to laugh at.

There were no bars either — the government had closed them, or God had, depending on who you asked. So we made our own. We'd drive to the half-built hotel on the ridge, the one abandoned when the money vanished, and we'd climb to the ninth floor where there were no walls yet, only concrete and the open dark. Mische always brought the gin. Adaeze brought cigarettes she stole from her father's driver, who pretended not to notice because we were the kind of girls you did not notice out loud.

We'd sit with our legs over the edge, nine floors of nothing beneath us, and we'd watch the city with its scattered fires. No streetlights. Just the small orange constellations of people cooking, praying, surviving. From up there it was beautiful. That was the sin of it. From up there everything terrible was beautiful.

"You could fall," Ines said once, to no one.

"That's the point," Mische answered, and passed the bottle.

We were not good girls. I want to be honest, because the story deserves it. We took things. Not because we needed them — we needed nothing, that was our whole disease — but because taking felt like touching. We'd walk through the market with our diplomatic faces on, untouchable, and slip fruit into our bags, ribbons, once a live chicken that Adaeze named General and released on the ambassador's lawn. We tipped in money that meant nothing to us and everything to them, and we felt like saints doing it, and we were wrong to feel that way, and we knew we were wrong, and we did it anyway. That was the whole arithmetic of us.

The boy came in the wet season.

He worked the checkpoints — one of the soldiers, maybe seventeen, with a rifle he held like it embarrassed him. He would wave the Mercedes through without looking because you did not look. But Mische made the driver stop once, rolled down the bulletproof glass she was never supposed to open, and offered him a cigarette.

He looked at her the way you look at weather you can't survive.

After that we saw him at the edges of things. And I understood, even then, that we were not being kind to him. We were feeding on him. His wanting was a warm thing and we were always cold, up there in our glass and our air conditioning. We passed him between us like the gin bottle. Ines cried about it later, which I thought was the greatest cruelty of all — to take a boy's whole heart and then weep as though the loss were yours.

I don't know what happened to him. That's the truth the story is built around. One week the checkpoint had a different face at it, younger even, and none of us asked. You did not ask. Asking was for people who intended to do something with the answer.

We left before the dry season came again. We always left. That was our nature — we were weather, we were the passing kind. Our fathers signed the last things and we folded ourselves back into the Mercedes and rode to the airport past the dry cathedrals of the pumps, past the market, past the ridge where the unfinished hotel still reached up with its concrete fingers into a sky that owed us nothing and gave us everything anyway.

I think about the ninth floor. The open edge. How we never fell, not one of us, though we deserved to more than anyone in that whole thirsty city.

That's the thing nobody tells you about being one of the bad girls.

The ground never comes for the ones who ought to meet it.

It comes for the boy at the checkpoint. It comes for the men beside the pumps.

We just drove away, cool and clean and terrible, and the glass kept everything out.

Even the sound of our own leaving.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a prose poem that mixes luxury, danger, and boredom—French wine, stolen cigarettes, empty streets patrolled by carless police—through the eyes of a wealthy teenager on a tropical coast.
counterfactuals.output:
**Riviera of the Idle Dead**

The wine is French, of course—everything worth drinking crossed an ocean to arrive at our indifference. I pour it into a glass Mother imported from somewhere with a name I never bothered to learn, and it catches the light like something bleeding beautifully. Château this. Domaine that. It tastes, if I'm honest, like every other afternoon: expensive and slightly sour, the color of a wound going purple.

The cigarettes I stole from the gardener, who steals them from someone poorer still. That's the economy down here—theft flowing uphill toward money, money flowing nowhere at all. I don't even like the smoke. I like the *taking*. I like the small red coal I hold against the enormous indifferent blue, this one hot point of rebellion in a life padded with silk and nothing to push against.

Below the villa, the streets lie empty as a laid table before guests arrive. The police walk them on foot now—no cars, no gas, or maybe just no reason—two men in damp uniforms patrolling boulevards where nothing happens to no one. They look up sometimes, at these white houses stacked like sugar cubes into the hills, and I wonder if they hate us, or if they've grown as bored as I have, both of us waiting for a crime worth the name.

The sea keeps making its promises. Palm trees rattle their dry applause for a performance that never begins.

I am seventeen and I have everything, which is a way of saying I have discovered the specific weight of nothing—how it settles in the throat like unswallowed wine, how it burns slow and sweet as a cigarette you don't want, how it patrols the perimeter of your gorgeous, guarded, absolutely empty days.

Somewhere a dog barks. The heat lies over the coast like a hand over a mouth.

I light another. I pour another. The afternoon does not end so much as forget to continue.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
